x.A: Snowcone is a physical device that takes days to ship and holds a small amount of data, so it can't move 30 TB within 5 days to FSx.
x.B: FSx File Gateway gives on-premises access to FSx file systems. It isn't a migration service that controls bandwidth.
x.C: DataSync is built for fast, parallel transfers to FSx for Windows File Server and lets you set a bandwidth limit, so the shared 1 Gbps link isn't overloaded. 30 TB can be done within 5 days.
x.D: Transfer Family provides SFTP, FTPS, and FTP access to S3 or EFS, and it isn't a migration tool for FSx for Windows.

x.A: CloudFront caches the videos at edge locations and delivers them close to users, which reduces buffering and scales without extra servers.
x.B: Replicating the videos across Regions with DataSync doesn't shrink the large raw files, and it adds cost and operations.
x.C: Elastic Transcoder converts the raw videos into formats and sizes suited to mobile devices, with no servers to manage.
x.D: EC2 instances in Local Zones for caching means running and scaling servers, which is a lot of overhead.
x.E: A fleet of EC2 instances for transcoding has to be managed and scaled, which Elastic Transcoder avoids.

x.A: EC2 Auto Scaling scales EC2 instances, not Fargate tasks, and scheduled scaling doesn't follow real utilization.
x.B: A Lambda function that scales ECS would be custom code that has to be built and maintained.
x.C: EC2 Auto Scaling doesn't apply to Fargate tasks, which are scaled with Application Auto Scaling.
x.D: Application Auto Scaling target tracking adjusts the number of Fargate tasks to hold CPU or memory near a target, scaling out at launch traffic and back in when utilization drops, which saves cost.

x.A: DataSync transfers data between NFS file systems in different Regions, including on a schedule, and handles the copying, verification, and retries with little setup.
x.B: Snowball devices are physical, and shipping them back and forth between Regions is slow and doesn't fit a periodic transfer.
x.C: An SFTP server on EC2 means building and managing servers and the transfer scripts.
x.D: DMS migrates databases, not NFS file systems.

x.A: DataSync copies data between locations and doesn't present a mountable file system for SMB clients.
x.B: A Windows file share on EC2 isn't fully managed, because you have to patch and manage the instance.
x.C: FSx for Windows File Server is fully managed and supports the SMB protocol, so SMB clients can use it.
x.D: S3 doesn't support SMB mounting directly, and an IAM role doesn't make a bucket a mountable SMB share.

x.A: A cluster placement group in a single AZ gives low latency and high network throughput between instances, and traffic within one AZ has no data transfer charges.
x.B: Using a partition strategy across AZs is for large distributed systems, and cross-AZ traffic costs money and adds latency.
x.C: An Auto Scaling group across AZs doesn't minimize latency or data transfer charges, and cross-AZ traffic is charged.
x.D: A step scaling policy across AZs has the same cross-AZ latency and charges.

x.A: S3 File Gateway presents files over NFS or SMB, not iSCSI block storage.
x.B: Tape Gateway is for virtual tape backups and doesn't provide primary iSCSI storage.
x.C: Stored volumes keep the complete data set on premises, so the company would still have to scale its local storage.
x.D: Cached volumes store the full data in S3 and keep only recently accessed data in a local cache, so the company doesn't need to scale local iSCSI storage.

x.A: Trusted Advisor checks cover the resources in the account where you view them, so the finance team has to look at the account where the RDS instances run.
x.B: The consolidated billing account's Trusted Advisor shows only its own resources, not all linked accounts' RDS checks.
x.C: The RDS Reserved Instance Optimization check isn't an available RDS check for this case, and the instances only run for 90 days, so reservations don't apply.
x.D: The RDS Idle DB Instances check finds instances with no connections, which helps cut costs from unused instances.
x.E: The Redshift Reserved Node check relates to Redshift, not RDS.

x.A: S3 Storage Lens advanced activity metrics show how buckets are accessed, so you can spot buckets with little or no activity, without building anything.
x.B: The S3 console dashboard shows basic information and doesn't give access pattern analysis.
x.C: The BucketSizeBytes metric shows size, not access, and Athena queries add setup work.
x.D: CloudTrail object-level logging with CloudWatch Logs is a lot to set up and costly, so it has high overhead.

x.A: Transfer Acceleration speeds up transfers over long distances but adds a per-GB fee, and it doesn't lower data transfer costs.
x.B: CloudFront caches the datasets at the edge for customers in North America and Europe, which lowers data transfer cost out of S3 and improves performance. CloudFront signed URLs keep access control.
x.C: A second bucket and replication add storage and replication costs and management, and don't reduce transfer charges by much.
x.D: Streaming through the web application sends all the data through the EC2 instances, which increases cost and reduces performance.

x.A: Kinesis streams per quote type need servers running the KCL to poll them, which means more infrastructure to manage.
x.B: A Lambda function per quote type with SNS doesn't store messages if processing fails, so quotes could be lost.
x.C: One SNS topic with SQS queues and message filtering routes each quote type to its own queue. SQS stores messages durably for days, so none are lost, and each backend processes its own queue.
x.D: Firehose delivering to OpenSearch and searching for messages is awkward, and it isn't a queue, so it has more maintenance.

x.A: A Lambda function that schedules snapshots is custom code and snapshots alone wouldn't back up the instance configuration.
x.B: An AWS Backup plan with the EC2 instances as resources backs up the instances' configuration (as AMIs) and their attached EBS volumes together, and it can copy the backups to another Region.
x.C: Adding only the EBS volumes backs up the data but not the EC2 instance configuration, so the application couldn't be fully recovered.
x.D: Copying to a different AZ doesn't provide recovery in a different Region.

x.A: A public bucket lets anyone watch the content, and KMS keys don't stream content or restrict viewers.
x.B: An IPsec VPN from every mobile device isn't practical for millions of users.
x.C: CloudFront delivers streaming content from edge locations at scale, and signed URLs limit access to authorized users.
x.D: Client VPN is for connecting individual users to a network, which doesn't scale to millions of mobile users.

x.A: Aurora MySQL requires choosing instance types and runs continuously, which costs more for infrequent access.
x.B: Aurora Serverless for MySQL scales capacity automatically and doesn't need an instance type chosen. It handles infrequent access cheaply and can grow with more users.
x.C: Redshift Spectrum queries S3 data from Redshift and isn't a MySQL database.
x.D: RDS for MySQL requires choosing an instance class.

x.A: Shield protects against DDoS attacks and doesn't scan for vulnerabilities.
x.B: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3, and it doesn't scan EC2 instances for vulnerabilities.
x.C: GuardDuty detects threats from logs and network activity. It isn't a vulnerability scanner for application weaknesses and doesn't use agents like that.
x.D: Inspector scans EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities and network exposure, and it generates findings that a Lambda function can turn into reports.

x.A: A larger instance costs more and still runs all the time, so it doesn't cut costs.
x.B: Turning the instance off when underutilized would stop message processing and isn't reliable for a growing queue.
x.C: A Lambda function triggered by the queue runs only when messages arrive, scales automatically as the queue grows, and costs nothing when the queue is empty.
x.D: Run Command runs scripts on instances on demand, but the instance still has to run, and the queue wouldn't be processed automatically.

x.A: A scheduled Glue ETL job converts the CSV files and loads them into Redshift, which the COTS application can query. It is serverless and low in overhead.
x.B: A Python script on EC2 means servers to manage, and the .sql files in S3 wouldn't be queryable by the COTS application.
x.C: DynamoDB isn't a data source the COTS application supports, since it works only with Redshift and S3.
x.D: A weekly EMR cluster is much heavier to manage than Glue, and the data would only be updated weekly.

x.A: CloudTrail records API calls, so it shows who launched oversized instances and changed security group rules, and when.
x.B: Data lifecycle policies manage EBS snapshots and have nothing to do with auditing configuration changes.
x.C: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations and doesn't track or audit configuration changes.
x.D: AWS Config tracks resource inventory and configuration changes over time, and rules can flag noncompliant settings such as oversized instances or open security groups.
x.E: Restoring configurations with CloudFormation fixes changes after the fact but doesn't track or audit them.

x.A: Session Manager gives secure access through IAM permissions with no SSH keys, no open ports, and no bastion hosts. It needs little administration across hundreds of instances.
x.B: STS generates temporary AWS credentials, not SSH keys, so this isn't a real feature.
x.C: Shared SSH access to bastion instances still relies on shared keys, which the security team wants removed.
x.D: A Cognito custom authorizer with Lambda generating SSH keys is a custom build with a lot of overhead.

x.A: Kinesis Data Streams durably stores the data so nothing is lost on a reboot, and Kinesis Data Analytics lets the team query it in near real time with SQL. It scales with the ingestion rate.
x.B: Firehose to Redshift buffers data before loading, so it isn't near real time, and it is heavier to run.
x.C: An instance store is lost on reboot, so the data-in-flight problem remains.
x.D: EBS and Redis pub/sub aren't a durable, queryable pipeline, because Redis channel messages aren't stored.

x.A: The x-amz-acl header sets object permissions, not encryption.
x.B: Requiring the ACL header to be private only controls access permissions and not encryption.
x.C: aws:SecureTransport enforces HTTPS for data in transit, not encryption of the objects at rest.
x.D: A bucket policy that denies PutObject requests without the x-amz-server-side-encryption header ensures every object uploaded is encrypted.

x.A: A Lambda function that generates the thumbnail and then alerts the user would make the user wait, since it isn't separating the confirmation from the long processing.
x.B: Step Functions can orchestrate but would still hold the confirmation until thumbnail generation finishes in this design, and it is heavier than needed.
x.C: Placing a message on an SQS queue for thumbnail generation decouples the work. The application confirms the upload right away while the thumbnails are generated asynchronously.
x.D: SNS to push a message only after thumbnail generation means the user isn't told promptly that the image was received.

x.A: A single EC2 instance as the HTTPS endpoint isn't highly available and has to be managed.
x.B: API Gateway provides a highly available HTTPS endpoint, Lambda processes each message, and DynamoDB stores the results for the security team. It is fully managed and scalable.
x.C: Route 53 only does DNS and can't invoke a Lambda function directly.
x.D: A VPN and S3 endpoint would not process the messages, and badge readers can't write to S3 this way over HTTPS messages.

x.A: An S3 File Gateway changes the protocol to NFS and requires modifying applications, and a 10 TB cache won't hold all the data for immediate access.
x.B: A tape gateway works with backup software and virtual tapes, which changes the existing infrastructure and doesn't keep file data available locally.
x.C: Cached volumes keep only part of the data locally, so users wouldn't have immediate local access to all file types without latency.
x.D: A stored volume gateway keeps the entire data set on premises for immediate low-latency access over iSCSI like today, and snapshots to AWS provide disaster recovery by restoring to an EBS volume.

x.A: A Cognito identity pool exchanges the user's token for temporary AWS credentials by assuming an IAM role. Updating it to assume the proper role gives users permission to access the protected bucket.
x.B: ACLs aren't how users authenticated with Cognito get access, and an ACL can't identify the temporary credentials from the identity pool.
x.C: S3 is now strongly consistent, so redeploying doesn't affect permissions and isn't the cause.
x.D: Custom attribute mappings pass attributes, but they don't grant permissions by themselves. The IAM role does.
